BUSINESS AUTOMATION CHECKLIST

10 Business Processes to Automate First.

Ten practical workflows businesses can evaluate first, plus a scorecard for choosing an automation project with measurable value.

By WeTakeFWDUpdated 28 November 202610 min read
IN THIS GUIDE1–3: enquiries, follow-up and appointments4–6: documents, invoices and data entry7–8: support and internal knowledge9–10: reporting and operational alertsScore each candidateProcesses not to automate firstTurn the winner into a pilotExplore business automation ↗

The first automation should not be the most impressive process. It should be the repeated process where a better flow creates visible value and manageable risk.

Use this list to find candidates, then score each one against volume, time, consistency, data readiness, exceptions and consequence. The best choice will be different for every business.

Key takeaways

  • Choose work with frequent repetition and a measurable baseline.
  • Fix unnecessary steps before automating them.
  • Prefer a bounded workflow with clear exceptions.
  • Measure the outcome, not the number of automated actions.

1–3: enquiries, follow-up and appointments

These workflows are good candidates because response time and missed opportunities are visible. Keep consent, frequency, escalation and customer preference central to the design.

  • Enquiry capture: place website, campaign and WhatsApp enquiries into one controlled queue.
  • Lead follow-up: assign ownership, prepare the next message and stop sequences when a person replies.
  • Appointments: confirm, remind and reschedule against real calendar availability.

4–6: documents, invoices and data entry

Do not allow uncertain extraction to silently change important records. Use confidence thresholds, validation and a review queue.

  • Document intake: extract fields and flag missing or uncertain information.
  • Invoice processing: match approved records and route exceptions for review.
  • System updates: move validated information between forms, spreadsheets, CRM and operational software.

7–8: support and internal knowledge

The prerequisite is trustworthy information. Conflicting documents and unclear ownership will produce conflicting answers regardless of the model used.

  • Routine support: answer from approved information and attach context to human handoffs.
  • Employee knowledge: search policies and procedures with citations to the maintained source.

9–10: reporting and operational alerts

Reporting automation should link numbers to sources. An alert needs an owner, urgency level and next action or it simply creates more noise.

  • Recurring reporting: assemble data from permitted sources and explain unusual changes.
  • Operational alerts: detect a defined condition, notify the right owner and track resolution.

Score each candidate

Give each workflow a score from one to five for frequency, staff time, delay, error, data readiness and ease of measurement. Then score risk, exception rate and integration complexity in the opposite direction. High-value, lower-risk candidates belong at the top of the pilot list.

  • How often does it happen?
  • How much handling time does it require?
  • What is lost when it is late or wrong?
  • Are the inputs reliable and accessible?
  • Can success be measured within 30–60 days?
  • Which cases must always go to a person?

Processes not to automate first

Avoid starting with rare workflows, poorly understood decisions, broad access to sensitive systems or tasks where an incorrect action has serious consequences. Do not automate a broken process merely to make the same confusion move faster.

  • High-stakes approvals without human review
  • Work with no agreed operating process
  • Sensitive data without clear permission and security ownership
  • Customer commitments based on unavailable information
  • A company-wide assistant with no defined job

Turn the winner into a pilot

When the pilot works, document the new operating process before expanding. Reliable automation is an operating capability, not a one-time installation.

  1. Name the workflow owner and desired outcome.
  2. Record the current baseline.
  3. Draw the trigger, steps, systems and exceptions.
  4. Remove steps that create no value.
  5. Build with narrow access and human escalation.
  6. Run under supervision and compare against the baseline.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

Good to know

What is the easiest process to automate?+

Structured, repeated work with reliable inputs and a clear outcome is usually easiest. Examples include routing enquiries, reminders and recurring reports.

Should every repetitive task be automated?+

No. Low-volume tasks may cost more to automate than they save, and some work benefits from human context or relationship.

How many workflows should a business automate at once?+

Start with one or a small connected set. Prove ownership, measurement and support before expanding to more systems.
